object_types.name: Account
object_types.definition: A customer account in the system. Every account has a unique, non-reusable account number and can hold subscriptions to products.

source_references.excerpt: An account. Every account has an account number. That's what everything hangs off.
Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: Subscription
object_types.definition: An agreement that an account pays a specified amount on a billing cycle for a product. Identified by subscription ID.

source_references.excerpt: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID.
Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: SubscriptionID
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for a subscription, generated and prefixed with SUB.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a subscription ID.
Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: AccountNumber

source_references.excerpt: Every account has an account number.

object_types.name: Product
object_types.definition: A product that can be subscribed to. Currently three products exist: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: PricePlan
object_types.definition: A billing artifact that specifies what a customer pays and how often. Identified by plan code (e.g., CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490). Each price plan points to exactly one feature bundle.

source_references.excerpt: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: PlanCode
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for a price plan.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a plan code

object_types.name: FeatureBundle
object_types.definition: A feature bundle that defines what a customer gets: the feature set including number of seats, API access, SSO, etc. Identified by name (Starter, Professional, Enterprise).

source_references.excerpt: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle -- how many seats, whether they get the API, whether they get SSO.
Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me.

object_types.name: BundleName
object_types.definition: The name uniquely identifying a feature bundle.

source_references.excerpt: Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's exactly one Professional.

object_types.name: PlanChange
object_types.definition: A record of a change in the price plan of a subscription. Has a change ID and records the subscription, new price plan, effective date, and requester.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record. We don't overwrite the plan on the subscription, we write a plan change with an effective date, and the subscription's current plan is derived from the change history. So a plan change is its own thing, with its own identity? It's got a change ID. It has to, because we need to know who made it and when it takes effect, and those are different dates.

object_types.name: ChangeID
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for a plan change.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: StartDate
object_types.definition: The date on which a subscription begins.

source_references.excerpt: Start date.
Start date is always there. You can't create a subscription without one, the form won't submit.

object_types.name: EndDate
object_types.definition: The date on which a subscription ends. Optional; open-ended subscriptions have no end date.

source_references.excerpt: End date, sometimes.
An open-ended subscription has no end date. Most of them are open-ended -- they run until cancelled.

object_types.name: BillingPeriod
object_types.definition: The billing cycle for a subscription.

source_references.excerpt: Monthly or annual.
Only those two. There was a quarterly once, for one customer, and it caused so much trouble that we bought them out of it.

ambiguities.description: Overloaded term 'Plan': The transcript uses 'plan' to refer to three distinct concepts: (1) 'Price Plan' or 'Billing Plan' - the pricing artifact with code like CORE-MO-49; (2) 'Feature Bundle' or 'Product Plan' - the feature tier like Starter/Professional/Enterprise; (3) a third meaning used by the sales team for negotiated deals. The model separates these into PricePlan and FeatureBundle entities, but stakeholders continue to use 'plan' ambiguously in conversation, which could cause confusion during implementation and maintenance.

source_references.excerpt: Priya, what's a plan? The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing. Tom: That's not what I mean by plan at all.

When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle -- how many seats, whether they get the API, whether they get SSO. It's the thing on the pricing page. We've got two things both called plan, and the sales team calls a third thing a plan, which is the deal they negotiated, which frequently matches neither.
Only that we still call three different things "plan" and this document won't fix that. It won't. But it'll at least name them separately, which is a start.

ambiguities.description: Identification of FeatureBundle: FeatureBundle is identified by a name (Starter, Professional, Enterprise) which is unique but not a traditional code or number. While the transcript confirms uniqueness ("There's exactly one Professional"), it also notes that there is no formal code for feature bundles ("There's no code, which annoys me"). The use of a natural language name as the primary identifier is atypical and may present challenges in systems that prefer numeric or alphanumeric codes.

source_references.excerpt: Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me. Is the name unique? Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

ambiguities.description: Mid-term annual subscription cancellation policy: The transcript reveals a discrepancy between stated policy and actual practice. The system rule is that cancellation on an annual subscription sets the end date to the paid-through date with no refund mechanism. However, four manual refunds were issued in the past quarter (described by Tom as 'goodwill' by Priya but characterized by Tom as indicating an unwritten policy). The facilitator explicitly parks this as undecided: "whether the system rule is the business rule" is unresolved, and the commercial treatment (run to term, prorated refund, or credit) requires decision by finance and legal. For now, the model captures the system behavior only.

source_references.excerpt: Tom: Mid-term cancellation on annual plans. Someone signs an annual deal in January, pays up front, cancels in April. What happens? Priya: Nothing happens. They've paid for the year, they keep access until December, we don't refund. Tom: That's not what the pricing page implies and it's not what sales tell people. ... Then I'm parking it explicitly. What happens commercially when an annual subscription is cancelled mid-term -- run to term, prorated refund, or credit -- is undecided.

ambiguities.description: Paused subscription status: Tom mentions a 'paused' status for subscriptions, but Priya clarifies it is not a formal status but rather a separate boolean flag. However, it behaves like a status in practice and causes bugs (e.g., active subscriptions returned by queries include paused ones). The model captures the four formal statuses (Trialing, Active, Past Due, Cancelled) as specified by Priya and Finance, but the existence and behavior of the paused flag is noted as an overlapping concern that may need separate modeling or constraint rules.

source_references.excerpt: Tom: There's also paused. Priya: Paused isn't a status, it's a flag. Tom: It behaves like a status. Priya: It behaves like a status but it isn't one, it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs. If you ask the system for active subscriptions you get paused ones too. Facilitator: I'm going to record the four statuses as the status, and note that paused exists separately and overlaps confusingly. I'm not going to invent a fifth status you don't have.

ambiguities.description: Subscription lifecycle and plan change history semantics: The transcript clarifies that a Subscription has a denormalised 'current plan' field that is maintained by the change process, and the plan change records form the authoritative history. However, if these two ever disagree, the change history is the source of truth and the current plan value is considered a bug. The model captures both the current plan on Subscription and the PlanChange records, but this implies that the current plan is a derived/cached value, not a primary fact. This creates a potential consistency issue: should the current plan be modeled as a view/computed value rather than a stored attribute, or should a constraint enforce their synchronization? The choice affects system design and auditing.

source_references.excerpt: Sam: You said a subscription belongs to one price plan. It doesn't, really -- that's what the plan changes are for. Priya: No, Sam, it does have a current plan field. The changes are the history, but there's a denormalised current plan on the record. Sam: Since when? Priya: Since the reporting rebuild. It's maintained by the change process, nobody sets it by hand. ... So the subscription does carry a current price plan, and the change records are the history behind it. Priya: Correct. And if those two ever disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug.

ambiguities.description: Product catalog scope: The transcript states there are currently three products (CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT), described as 'fixed today,' and mentions a fourth product in discovery. The ProductCode value type is constrained to these three values in the model, but this constraint may become stale as new products are added. It is unclear whether the value constraint should be maintained dynamically in the model or treated as documentation of the current state only.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT. Fixed at three? Fixed today. There's a fourth in discovery, but I'm not going to pretend I know what it is.

ambiguities.description: FeatureBundle identification and lifecycle: The transcript indicates that a FeatureBundle (e.g., Enterprise) can exist without any PricePlan pointing to it. The example given is that Enterprise existed for two months with no pricing available to customers. This means the model allows FeatureBundle to be created independently of any PricePlan, which is valid, but it also means that in reporting or product management, there could be 'orphan' bundles with no associated pricing. It is unclear whether there should be a business rule that eventually every bundle must have at least one price plan, or if the current model correctly allows temporary bundles.

source_references.excerpt: And can a bundle exist with no price plan pointing at it? Yes -- we build a bundle before we price it. Enterprise existed for two months before there was anything to buy.

ambiguities.description: Email and contact identification: The transcript mentions that email is a field on the 'contact,' not directly on the account. It is not clear whether a separate Contact entity type should be modeled, or whether the contact information is out of scope for this model. The question of whether email uniquely identifies an account (or is optional) is unanswered.

source_references.excerpt: Is there anything else that identifies an account? Email, company name? Company name absolutely not, we have four accounts called "Acme." Email is on the contact, not the account.

ambiguities.description: Plan change request date vs. effective date distinction: The transcript notes that the date a change is requested and the date it takes effect can differ (e.g., a change requested on the 3rd but effective on the 1st of next month). The model captures EffectiveDate on PlanChange but does not capture a 'RequestedDate' or 'ChangeDate' (the date the change record was created/made). It is unclear whether RequestedDate should be a separate attribute or is implicit in the system metadata.

source_references.excerpt: It has to, because we need to know who made it and when it takes effect, and those are different dates. Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month.
